title: Modbus
summary: Modbus is a simple, openly published industrial communication protocol, introduced in 1979, that lets a controlling device read and write data in industrial equipment. It uses a client and server model, historically called master and slave: one device polls and the others answer, and there is no peer to peer conversation. Requests carry a function code that names the operation and an address in a flat register space, covering coils for single bits and holding or input registers for 16 bit values, with addressing quirks between the classic serial form and the TCP form. Modbus runs over serial links such as RS-485 in the RTU and ASCII variants, and over TCP, conventionally on port 502. The security property that matters is that the protocol itself provides no authentication, no encryption, no integrity checking and no replay protection, so any host that can reach the service and form a valid request can command equipment, and responses can be spoofed or replayed. These were deliberate trade offs for deterministic, low cost local control, not oversights. Defensive practice therefore lives around the protocol: strict segmentation, one way or brokered traffic through a protocol aware gateway, access control lists, read only paths where a control action is unnecessary, passive monitoring to baseline which function codes and registers are normal, and change control that keeps unauthorised writes out. The common mistake is assuming a gateway or an industrial firewall can be made to validate identity at the protocol level, when the real control is which network paths exist and who may use them.

beginner.definition: Modbus is a rule set that industrial devices use to talk to each other. One device asks a question, and the others answer with readings or accept a command. It was designed to be simple and cheap, so it sends plain data with no passwords. It is often shortened to Modbus TCP when it runs over ordinary networks, and Modbus RTU when it runs over a serial cable.
beginner.whyItMatters: Modbus has no way to check who is asking. Any device that can reach it can read values and, in many setups, write commands. There is no encryption, so anyone on the path can watch or copy the messages. A simple wrong command can open a valve or stop a pump. Because you cannot add a password to the protocol itself, safety depends on the network around it.
howItWorks: A controlling device sends a request that names a function code, which is the type of operation.
The request also names an address in a flat list of registers, which are small numbered storage slots.
Simple bits are stored as coils, and 16 bit values are stored in holding or input registers.
The target device performs the action and sends a short reply containing the requested values.
There is no login step, so the message itself is the whole proof of authority.
Engineers protect it with separate networks, firewall rules, gateways and constant monitoring for odd writes.
beginner.example: Picture a block of flats with a shared boiler in the basement. Each flat has a small dial to set its own heating, and one caretaker walks around reading meters. The dials have no locks, because everyone in the building was assumed to be friendly. So the safety of the boiler depends entirely on who can enter the basement. If a stranger gets in, they can turn every dial and no one will stop them. The caretaker's notebook of normal readings is the only clue that something changed. A locked basement door is the real protection, not a cleverer dial.
takeaways: Modbus carries no password, no encryption and no way to verify the sender.
Protection comes from network separation, gateways and strict firewall rules, not from the protocol.
Baseline normal traffic so that unusual register writes stand out quickly.

objectives: Describe what Modbus is and the client and server model it uses.
Explain the meaning of function codes, coils and registers in simple terms.
State the security properties Modbus lacks, including authentication, encryption and replay protection.
Describe defensive measures such as segmentation, gateways, access rules and write restrictions.
Explain how passive monitoring and baselining help detect unexpected Modbus activity.
